title: Finding Sita
hookLine: the ashoka grove; Rama's story sung softly from a tree; the ring
last: NO REST TILL RAMA'S WORK IS DONE.

lines: A CITY OF GOLD, AT NIGHT.
cards: Lanka at night: a city of gold, full of music, feasting and guards. Hanuman shrinks to the size of a cat and searches, palace after palace, room after room.
He sees the demon king Ravana's wives asleep, and for a moment wonders if one is Sita. Then he stops himself. No.
Sita would never sleep peacefully here. He almost gives up. Then, at the city's edge, a grove of ashoka trees.
Under one tree, guarded by fierce women, sits a woman in a single worn cloth, thin from grief, refusing everything she's offered. He climbs into the branches above her and waits.

teach.b: Hanuman has a problem. If a giant monkey drops out of a tree in the enemy's city and says Rama sent me, she'll scream, and he'll be caught. So he does something gentle.
Hidden in the leaves, he softly tells Rama's story, the one she knows best. Sita looks up.
He comes down, bows, and gives her proof of who he is: Rama's ring. She holds it, the text says, with joy, as though she'd found her husband again.

teach.h: CLIMB ON MY BACK. SHE SAYS NO.
teach.b: Then Hanuman offers: climb on my back, and I'll carry you across the ocean tonight. But in Valmiki, Sita says no.

She won't willingly touch any man but her husband, and she wants Rama to come himself and end this properly. She gives Hanuman a jewel from her hair, and a small private story only Rama would know. Ring in, jewel out.
Now look at how Hanuman first reached her. Not with strength. With Rama's story, sung softly from a tree.
Hearing it, she knew a friend was near.
Hindu teachers count this as devotion: in a well-known list of nine ways of bhakti, the first is shravana, simply hearing God's story.
That's why families sit through long Ramayana readings, and grandparents tell these stories at bedtime. The story is how hope gets into a guarded place.

how: The scene of Hanuman giving Rama's ring to Sita in the ashoka grove is often painted and performed, and it's a high point when devotees recite the Sundara Kanda.

o: Hanuman's search of Lanka, ending with a ring in a garden
Hanuman carrying the princess home across the ocean on his back
Rama's army storming Ravana's golden city to win her back

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: in Valmiki, Sita escapes on Hanuman's back
she declines. she wants Rama to come himself.
Hanuman first reaches Sita by telling Rama's story softly
so she won't be frightened when he appears.
Hindu teachers count simply hearing God's story as a way of devotion
shravana, hearing, comes first in a well-known list of nine ways of bhakti.

games.q: you're Sita. a messenger from Rama offers to carry you across the ocean tonight. what do you do?
o: climb on his back and go.
stay, and send a jewel so Rama comes himself.
ask him to bring Rama's army first, then decide.
games.why: in Valmiki she says no: she won't willingly touch another man, and she wants Rama to come and end this. she sends her hair jewel back.

practice: Sit and breathe. Bring back one moment from this week's story that stayed with you: the baby and the sun, the old bear at the shore, the ring. Hear it again in your mind, slowly, the way Sita heard it from the tree.
If you pray, let the hearing be your prayer. If you don't, just notice what it stirs in you.

wordCard.voice: Finding Sita. In the ashoka grove: Rama's story sung from a tree, his ring in, her hair jewel out.

orig.note: Sanskrit: crest jewel, the hair ornament Sita sends back to Rama.

carryVoice: Your line: hearing God's story is devotion. Sita heard it from a tree. Day thirty-three, done.
